items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: And then I had an opportunity to see Duke Ellington close up and to see Johnny Hodges and Sonny Greer.

ctx.x: Well, Fats had so many things going...

All right. Fats, he was on the radio. See, Fats used to come over a radio station in Cincinnati, or someplace. And really have an opportunity to play. Plus he could play. And then, too, you know, you gotta remember that a lot of these musicians had managers that were in the way. The managers were just in the way, so they prevented the man from really playing, you know, like he could play. Thinking like he could think. You know, a hundred dollars would really change a guy's mind.

items.q: I'm going to be in touch with the Congressman from this District and his assistant to see if we can't induce the New York School System to introduce in their curriculum Black Music History, with Duke and Louis and myself and others

ctx.x: And then you did a book for...

Edward B. Marks, yeah, called In Boogie-Woogie Land. And I played some original tunes and have a sketch to show the illustrations and demonstrations. But what I wanted to do more than anything, and I'm going to be in touch with the Congressman from this District and his assistant to see if we can't induce the New York School System to introduce in their curriculum Black Music History, with Duke and Louis and myself and others, and so that when a kid go to the music class and hear Copland, he can hear Duke. He can…

years ago we got them to invite an astronaut to come to Harlem, which they did, and gave the black kids an opportunity to see a black astronaut and to know that a black man can be involved in the space program.

items.q: Duke and Lucky Millinder and Cab Calloway and, of course, Count Basie hadn't left Kansas City then.

ctx.x: So a lot of bands came through...

A lot of bands came through Detroit and played the Fox Theater. You see, again I said, shows were factors. Shows were the principal items and the musicians...Of course, they would begin that transition period of...from shows to just having...they'd have like a vaudeville--five acts--and maybe the principal act would be the band. Duke and Lucky Millinder and Cab Calloway and, of course, Count Basie hadn't left Kansas City then. He didn't leave Kansas City until...
